title: Integration by Parts
summary: Integration by parts reverses the product rule: $\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du$. Choosing $u$ (to differentiate) and $dv$ (to integrate) wisely — often by the LIATE guide — turns products like $x e^x$ and $x\ln x$ into simpler integrals.

integration by parts.plain: A rule for integrating a product of functions.
integration by parts.in_class: $\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du$; reverses the product rule.

LIATE.plain: A guide for choosing $u$: Log, Inverse-trig, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential.
LIATE.in_class: Pick $u$ as the earliest type on the list.

u and dv.plain: The two pieces you split the integrand into.

reduction formula.plain: Applying parts to lower a power step by step.
reduction formula.in_class: e.g. reduces $\int x^n e^x\,dx$ each round.

cyclic integral.plain: Parts loops back to the original integral.
cyclic integral.in_class: Solve algebraically for the integral (e.g. $\int e^x\sin x$).

product rule reversed.plain: The origin of the parts formula.

choosing wisely.plain: Good $u$/dv makes the new integral easier.
choosing wisely.in_class: Aim for a $\int v\,du$ simpler than the original.

concept_sections.heading: The formula
concept_sections.explanation: From the product rule, $\int u\,dv=uv-\int v\,du$. Split the integrand into a part to differentiate ($u$) and a part to integrate ($dv$).
math_steps: Choose $u$ and $dv$ so $u\,dv$ is the integrand.

concept_sections.heading: Choosing $u$ with LIATE
concept_sections.explanation: Pick $u$ as the function type appearing earliest in LIATE (Log, Inverse-trig, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential); the rest is $dv$. This usually makes $\int v\,du$ simpler.

concept_sections.heading: Algebraic × exponential/trig
concept_sections.explanation: For $\int x e^x\,dx$ or $\int x\cos x\,dx$, choose $u=x$ (differentiates to a constant) so one round of parts finishes the job.

concept_sections.heading: Logarithms and inverse trig
concept_sections.explanation: For $\int\ln x\,dx$ or $\int\arctan x\,dx$, let $u$ be the log/inverse-trig (there's no obvious antiderivative) and $dv=dx$.

concept_sections.heading: Repeat and cyclic cases
concept_sections.explanation: Sometimes parts must be applied twice (reduction), or it cycles back to the original integral — then solve for it algebraically, as with $\int e^x\sin x\,dx$.
math_steps: Apply parts once; if still a product, apply again.
If the original reappears, set the equation.

real_world_examples.title: Work by a spring-like force
real_world_examples.scenario: Force times distance where force depends on position.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Products like $x\,e^{-x}$ arise and integrate by parts to give total work.

real_world_examples.title: Expected value in probability
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: $\int x e^{-x}\,dx$ (an expected value) is a textbook integration-by-parts.

real_world_examples.title: Signal energy
real_world_examples.scenario: Combining a ramp with an oscillation.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: $\int x\sin x\,dx$-type integrals appear and are solved by parts.
